clue.text: Construction worker moans about a few pounds put on

indicators.note: one piece is set on in front of the other, building the word from the weight first

parts.note: a stone is a British weight of fourteen pounds

indicators.note: the letters of moans are turned about into a new order

explanation.surface: A builder grumbles that he has gained a little weight.
explanation.walkthrough: A stone is a British unit of weight, fourteen pounds; 'about' is the anagram signal on 'moans', and 'put on' places the weight first.
explanation.definitionFit: A stonemason cuts and lays stone, a skilled trade on building sites.

clue.text: Start to organise pastries about to surround higher layer

indicators.note: the word for the pastries is turned about, read from right to left

parts.note: tarts are pastries

indicators.note: the start of the next word, its opening letter, is all that is taken

parts.note: to sphere is to enclose or encircle, as if in a globe

explanation.surface: A baker is told to begin arranging pastries around a top tier of a cake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' turns the pastries round; 'Start to' takes the opening of 'organise', which the setter slots in after them without signalling the order. To sphere, meaning to encircle, is a genuine dictionary verb.
explanation.definitionFit: The stratosphere is the band of atmosphere above the troposphere, a higher level of the air.

clue.text: She's common but not all there

indicators.note: the word is not all present: its final letter is missing

parts.note: normal means ordinary, common

explanation.surface: A woman is dismissed as ordinary and a bit dim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not all there' (slang for dim) here means the word for 'common' loses its last letter, L. 'She' defines a girl's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Norma is a woman's name, so a 'she' in crossword terms.

clue.text: Swimmer one caught leaving calm creek distressed

indicators.note: upset, so the remaining letters are thrown into disorder
the letter for caught departs from the words before the shuffle

parts.note: C is the cricket abbreviation for caught; one of the two Cs in the fodder goes

explanation.surface: A fish is hooked and lifted from a quiet inlet in a state of panic.
explanation.walkthrough: CALM CREEK has two Cs; 'leaving' removes one (C for caught), and 'distressed' rearranges the remaining ALMCREEK.
explanation.definitionFit: A mackerel is a fish, a swimmer of the sea.

clue.text: Shake up new lotto arrangement to make it silly

indicators.note: an arrangement of the letters puts them in a fresh order

explanation.surface: Someone proposes reshuffling a lottery draw to make it daft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shake up' looks like the anagram signal but is part of the fodder; 'arrangement' is the signal over all fifteen letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone slow to understand is dim, which is what silly means in this sense.

clue.text: Shelter from swirling sleet after end of rain

indicators.note: the shuffled weather word comes after the single letter
the final letter of the word rain is used
the letters of sleet whirl round into a new order

explanation.surface: A walker seeks cover from whirling sleet once the rain stops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'swirling' is the anagram signal on 'sleet', placed 'after' the end of 'rain'; 'Shelter' is a verb here.
explanation.definitionFit: To nestle is to settle snugly and protected, as a bird sheltering in a nest.

clue.text: Rubbish say, put up round part of 29

indicators.note: the reversed pair goes round the other piece
in a down clue, putting up means reading the letters from the bottom

parts.note: e.g. means for example, which 'say' also signals
a rung is one step of a ladder, part of the answer to 29-across

explanation.surface: Junk is hoisted up around a section of the ladder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put up' turns the abbreviation for 'say' upwards in this down clue, and 'round' wraps it about one step of the ladder at 29-across.
explanation.definitionFit: Grunge is grime or dirt, a slang word for rubbish.

clue.text: Haggard's book about old Oxford, perhaps

indicators.note: the book title goes about, around, the letter for old

parts.note: She is a novel by H. Rider Haggard

explanation.surface: A discussion of a Victorian adventure novel set in the old university city.
explanation.walkthrough: H. Rider Haggard's novel SHE goes 'about' O. 'Oxford' is not the city but a lace-up shoe, and 'perhaps' marks it as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: An Oxford is a style of laced leather shoe, one kind of footwear.

clue.text: Planet towards end of galaxy appears blue

indicators.note: the planet comes up to, beside, the single letter

parts.note: Earth is a planet

indicators.note: the final letter of galaxy is used

explanation.surface: A planet near the edge of the galaxy looks blue from space.
explanation.walkthrough: 'blue' means smutty, not the colour: EARTHY in its coarse sense. 'end of' gives Y from 'galaxy'.
explanation.definitionFit: Earthy humour is crude and bawdy, which is what blue means of jokes.

clue.text: They take back surgical instruments

explanation.surface: People withdrawing claims are compared to tools in an operating theatre.
explanation.definitionFit: Those who retract withdraw statements, and in surgery a retractor holds back tissue or an incision's edges.

clue.text: Green form of transport is what's used in central Guatemala?

definitions.text: Green form of transport is what's used in central Guatemala?

parts.words: Green form of transport is what's used in central Guatemala?
parts.note: an eco-friendly vehicle, described by the middle letters of the country's name, T then E and M, spoken as a phrase

explanation.surface: A question about the eco-friendly vehicle favoured in Central America.
explanation.walkthrough: GUATEMALA's centre holds T, E, M; said as 'T and EM' these letters give the answer, so 'central Guatemala' points to letters, not the region.
explanation.definitionFit: A tandem is a bicycle for two riders, a pollution-free way to travel.

clue.text: New material broadcast at revue's opening is just the tonic!

indicators.note: the single letter is placed at the end of the anagram
broadcast means scattered widely, so the letters are strewn into a new order
the opening letter of the word revue's is taken

explanation.surface: Fresh content aired at the start of a show is just what the audience needed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broadcast' rearranges NEW MATERIAL as MINERALWATE, followed by R, the 'opening' of 'revue's'. 'Tonic' puns on tonic water.
explanation.definitionFit: Bottled spring water is drunk as a restorative, and tonic water is a fizzy mixer.

clue.text: The short people in an ancient country

indicators.note: the word is cut short, losing its last letter

parts.note: a race is a people

explanation.surface: Folk living in a long-gone kingdom are described as short.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short' trims 'The' to TH. Thrace was an ancient region of south-east Europe.
explanation.definitionFit: Thrace was a historic region north of the Aegean, a land of antiquity.

clue.text: Note about substance used to make cheese

indicators.note: the word for the banknote is turned about, written backwards

parts.note: a tenner is a ten-pound banknote

explanation.surface: A musical comment on an ingredient in dairy production.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Note' suggests music but is a banknote, a TENNER (British for a £10 note), which 'about' reverses.
explanation.definitionFit: Rennet is the curdling enzyme added to milk in cheesemaking.

clue.text: Manage to hide tail of little pig

indicators.note: the last letter of the word is hidden from view, removed

parts.note: a runt is the smallest animal of a litter, typically a piglet

explanation.surface: A farmer tries to conceal a piglet's curly tail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to hide tail of' drops T from RUNT, the weakling of a litter.
explanation.definitionFit: To run a business is to manage it.

clue.text: It's not odd to follow the Spanish cardinal

indicators.note: the second piece follows, comes after, the first

parts.note: el is Spanish for the
a number that is not odd is even

explanation.surface: A remark about a Spanish churchman's even-handedness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cardinal' is a cardinal number, not a churchman.
explanation.definitionFit: Cardinal numbers are counting numbers such as one, two, and this one.

clue.text: Museum finally expel destructive member of the public

parts.note: the V&A, the Victoria and Albert Museum in London, read as V and A

indicators.note: the final letter of the word expel is taken

explanation.surface: A museum ejects a visitor who has damaged the exhibits.
explanation.walkthrough: The V&A is London's Victoria and Albert Museum, spelt out V AND A; 'finally' adds L from 'expel'.
explanation.definitionFit: A vandal wilfully damages property, a destructive citizen.

clue.text: New cheaper Pilsner could be something struggling writer might resort to

definitions.text: something struggling writer might resort to

indicators.note: the letters could be rearranged into something else

explanation.surface: A cut-price lager is touted as the answer for blocked authors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'could be' rearranges N (for 'New') with CHEAPER PILSNER. A struggling writer, here, is one whose pencil has gone blunt.
explanation.definitionFit: A blunt pencil writes badly, and the gadget that sharpens it gets the writing going again.

clue.text: Possum put bell on dog

indicators.note: in a down clue, the first piece is set on top of the second
in a down clue, the first piece is set on top of the second

parts.note: to ring is what a bell does, and a ring is a call on one
to dog someone is to follow or tail them

explanation.surface: Someone ties a bell to a dog's collar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dog' is the verb, to follow, which TAIL also means.
explanation.definitionFit: The ringtail is an Australian possum named for its curling tail.

clue.text: The top is missing from a navigational aid still in use

indicators.note: the first letter of the word is taken off

parts.note: a sextant is an instrument for navigation by the stars

explanation.surface: Sailors complain that the top part of their instrument has gone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The top is missing from' drops the first letter, S, from SEXTANT.
explanation.definitionFit: Something extant still exists, surviving and current.

clue.text: Request made to umpire after a soft sound of thunder

parts.note: p, piano, is the musical abbreviation for soft
a peal is a loud rolling crash, as of thunder

explanation.surface: A cricketer asks the umpire for a decision after a gentle rumble of thunder.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the fielders appeal to the umpire to give a batsman out. 'after' joins the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket, an appeal is the fielders' cry asking the umpire for a dismissal.

clue.text: Goodies are touring during dry season initially

indicators.note: the shuffled letters go in between the letters for dry

parts.note: TT, teetotal, means not drinking alcohol

indicators.note: the letters of are travel about, rearranged
the initial letter of the word season is taken

explanation.surface: Sweets are handed out on tour during the dry months.
explanation.walkthrough: 'touring' rearranges ARE as REA, which goes 'during' TT (teetotal); 'initially' adds S from 'season'.
explanation.definitionFit: Treats are special delights such as sweets, as goodies are.

clue.text: Spot rear of sailor in a French vessel

indicators.note: the single letter goes in the French article

parts.note: un is French for a

indicators.note: the last letter, at the back of the word sailor, is used

explanation.surface: Someone is asked to spot a sailor's backside on a French boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spot' only invites the solver to find the answer. 'rear of' gives R from 'sailor', which goes 'in' UN. 'vessel' suggests a ship but means a container.
explanation.definitionFit: An urn is a vase or container, a vessel in the sense of a pot.

clue.text: Industrial action leads to girls on strike losing other work

indicators.note: the leading letter of each of the following words is taken

explanation.surface: Female workers walk out over job losses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leads to' takes the first letters of 'girls on strike losing other work'. 'strike' points to a walkout, but the answer is a milder protest.
explanation.definitionFit: A go-slow is a protest where workers deliberately reduce output, a form of union pressure.

clue.text: Placed saw on radio

indicators.note: the word is spoken over the airwaves, so it is heard not read

parts.note: saw means spotted, sighted

explanation.surface: A carpenter's tool is put on the wireless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'saw' is the past tense of see, not the tool.
explanation.definitionFit: Something sited has been located or positioned.

clue.text: Pass first part of exam but with error

indicators.note: only the first letter of the word exam is used

parts.note: a lapse is a slip or mistake

explanation.surface: A student passes the first paper despite a mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pass' looks like an exam result but means to go by, as time does.
explanation.definitionFit: Time elapses when it passes by.

clue.text: Bloomer — perhaps made by large yob

parts.note: L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large
an oaf is a lout, a clumsy boor

explanation.surface: A blunder committed by a big lout.
explanation.walkthrough: A bloomer is a British crusty bread, so a loaf; 'Bloomer' tempts as a blunder. YOB is British slang for a loutish youth.
explanation.definitionFit: A bloomer is a crusty British bread, a kind of baked bread shape.

clue.text: Sadly abstain when entertaining bright Protestant

indicators.note: the shuffled letters entertain, hold within them, the other piece
sadly here means badly done, so the letters come out wrongly ordered

parts.note: apt means quick to learn, bright

explanation.surface: A gloomy teetotaller hosts a clever churchgoer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sadly' is the anagram signal on 'abstain', and 'entertaining' takes the word for bright inside. Anabaptists are a Reformation movement practising adult baptism.
explanation.definitionFit: The Anabaptists were a Reformation movement, and adherents hold to adult baptism within Protestantism.

clue.text: Rock club with girl in it

indicators.note: the girl's name goes in it, inside the word for club

parts.note: a bat is a club used in sport
Sal is a girl's name, short for Sally

explanation.surface: A nightclub admits a young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'club' suggests a nightclub but is a cricket BAT.
explanation.definitionFit: Basalt is a dark volcanic stone.

clue.text: Some exercise with 14 — this may help you get up

definitions.text: this may help you get up

parts.note: step is a form of aerobic exercise
14-across is a run, which in tights or stockings is a ladder

explanation.surface: A fitness routine is suggested to help someone rise in the morning.
explanation.walkthrough: In British English a ladder is a run in tights; 14-across is RUN.
explanation.definitionFit: A folding set of steps lets you climb to reach high places.
